newsitem.title: USA: APL to spin off some U.S. shipping opers..
newsitem.headline: APL to spin off some U.S. shipping opers..

text.p: U.S. container shipping company APL Ltd said Wednesday it will spin off a portion of its U.S. maritime business to a new privately-held company as part of APL's planned merger with Singapore-based Neptune Orient Lines Ltd.

APL also said it had filed a request with the U.S. Maritime Administration (MarAd) to transfer federal government subsidies for nine U.S.-flag vessels to the new company, which will be called American Ship Managment LLC.

ASM will be owned and operated independently of APL, but its top manangment will be drawn from current APL executives. ASM's new president, Jordan Truchan, now serves as APL's vice president of ocean transportation services.

In spinning off the operation of its U.S.-flag vessels, APL hopes to head off a potential loss of nearly $20 million in annual subsidies it receives under the Maritime Security Program, which maintains U.S.-flag ships with U.S. crews for military use during times of national emergency.
If MarAd approves the transfer of the subsidies, ASM will then time-charter the U.S.-flag vessels back to APL for its own use.

"The arrangements being implemented by APL and ASM meet the criteria specifically established by Congress under the Maritime Security Program (MSP) and by MarAd itself when we enrolled APL vessles in the Maritime Secuirty Fleet," APL president and CEO Timothy Rhein said in a statement.

APL's decision to spin off its U.S.-flag operations comes less than a week after MarAd turned down an application by bankrupt U.S. carrier Lykes Lines to transfer operating subsidies to its new owner, Canadian Pacific Ltd.
In its ruling, MarAd said that Lykes' proposed transfer of more than $6.0 million in annual subsidies would have resulted in "excessive foreign control" over U.S.-flag ships.
CP Ships said it still plans to go ahead with its $34 takeover of Lykes, which has been operating under Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection since October 1995.
In addition to the nine U.S.-flag ships, APL will also seek MarAd's approval to transfer to APL its contract to operate 12 vessels that are part of the U.S. Ready Reserve Force.

In April, NOL announced its plan to acquire San Francisco, California-based APL in a deal valued at more than $800 million. Under the terms of the agreement, NOL will pay $33.50 per share for all 24.6 million outstanding shares of APL, the second-biggest container company in the U.S.
APL, which will become a fully-owned subsidiary of NOL, expects the merger to completed sometime in the fall.
Shipping analysts have said the CP-Lykes decision could spell trouble for the impending NOL-APL marriage.

While MarAd stressed in its ruling that every case involving foreign participants in U.S.-flag companies will be decided on its merits, analysts said the decision could reflect MarAd's misgivings over foreign takeovers of U.S. carriers who participate in the maritime security fleet.
APL downplayed the similarities between the two applications, saying its proposal meets the conditions of the U.S. subsidy program set down by MarAd in a letter to APL earlier this year.

"We feel that we have good chance of getting our approval," said new ASM head Truchan. "MarAd gave a positive indication that they would give approval to an organization like this, and we feel that we will able to work this out."
The newly-formed ASM will be mostly employee-held, Truchan said, and is pursuing financing through banking institutions.
"We are seeking some outside investors but we have not identified any particular ones yet," he said.
MarAd acknowledged the receipt of APL's proposal, but has yet to give any indication on when it issue its decision.
((Wendy Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640))
